newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Petrobras, YPF in search of new promising markets.
newsitem.headline: Petrobras, YPF in search of new promising markets.

text.p: Brazilian and Argentine oil and gas firms Petrobras and YPF SA have joined forces to gain new market shares and take advantage of Brazil's promising natural gas market, analysts said.

State-owned Petrobras and YPF have signed two agreements in Buenos Aires to set up a $730-million joint-venture in fuel distribution and to set up a $630-million gas production project together with Dow Chemical.

"The fuel distribution joint venture makes sense because Petrobras already has a 35-percent market share in Brazil and YPF has 41 percent of the Argentine market," said Oliver Mizne, oil analyst at Banco Garantia. "It would be difficult for either company to increase significantly its market share at home."
Mizne said Argentina was the most obvious market for Petrobras to move into next and vice versa given the countries' membership of the Mercosur customs union.

The 50-50 Petrobras-YPF venture will act in the purchase and resale of liquid and gas fuels, transportation, warehousing and refining of petroleum and petrochemical products and the import and export of petroleum products.
Marcia Garcez, oil analyst at Bozano, Simonsen, said Petrobras and YPF would not reap instant gains by entering each others markets but in the long-term their was potential for profit growth.

"To enter the fuel distribution market is very complicated because it is highly competitive," Garcez said. "It takes a long time to establish a reasonable market share but there is potential for long-term growth."
Analysts said with the gas production venture, known as Mega Project, the companies tried to position themselves to take advantage of Brazil's promising natural gas market.
Currently, gas accounts for only two percent of Brazilian energy consumption, but the government is promoting gas as a source of energy and wants it to account for 10 percent of consumption by 2005.
YPF's long-term growth strategy is to increase gas sales and exports, while Petrobras is aiming to secure a primary resource in an expanding market, analysts said.

"The future of YPF lies more with gas than with oil in the long term. The use of gas as an energy source is expanding more than the use of oil," said Hernan Ladeuix, head of research oil and gas at ING Barings in Buenos Aires.
He said most of the increase in YPF's gas production would be destined for export to Brazil and Chile.

The Mega Project, 38 percent owned by YPF, 34 percent by Petrobras and 28 percent by Dow Chemical, will develop natgas fields in Argentina's Neugina Basin with the construction of a liquid gas separation plant, a 375-mile (600 km) gas pipeline and a fractionating unit in the city of Bahia Blanca.

Garcez said Brazil was starting to use more gas, but did not have enough gas to guarantee the supply for the country's petrochemical industry. She said more partnerships like the Mega Project would be seen in the future to secure the supply of gas.

Once the Mega Project is up and running within three years, the project will produce about 516,000 tonnes a year of ethane, which Dow Chemical will use to expand production at its partly-owned petrochemical plant in Bahia Blanca.
Approximately 615,000 tonnes of liquified petroleum gas and 188,000 tonnes of primary gasoline will be exported each year to Brazil.
